articles.title: OpenAI's Astra Model Sparks AGI Speculation
articles.content: OpenAI slow-walks debut of delayed GPT-6, with Trusted Access Program participants getting first shot Thomas Claburn Thomas Claburn AI AND SOFTWARE REPORTER Published thu 3 Sep 2026 // 23:42 UTC OpenAI commits $1B in AI credits to frontline cyber defenders now True AI-pocalypse as ChatGPT, Claude, and Grok all go down at once 5 hours ago To keep the AI hacking genie bottled up, try one-way networks 17 hours ago With Gemini 3.8 Flash, Google reminds everyone it's still in the race 1 day ago Infosec pros say we're not ready to lose control of AI 1 day ago After a brief training pause to reflect on the inadequacy of its AI security measures, OpenAI has released GPT-6 Astra, initially for those in its Trusted Access Program. Assuming all goes well and there are no more incidents like the Hugging Face hack , the AI biz in a few days will allow Plus, Pro, Business, and Enterprise subscribers to try out what the company describes as "our most intelligent model yet, with state-of-the-art performance in computer use, browsing, software engineering, science, and professional work." GPT-6 Astra arrives just two days after rival Anthropic debuted Fable 5.1, at the same eye-watering price : $10 per million input tokens and $50 per million output tokens.  Astra, OpenAI says, is the first of its models to reach the "Critical" level for cybersecurity capabilities under its Preparedness Framework . The 22-page policy document has been  panned [PDF] by researchers, who argue that it "allows OpenAI’s CEO to deploy even more dangerous capabilities, especially if other AI developers do so." And here we are. OpenAI's cautionary but upbeat assessment of Astra describes it as "a significant step up in cyber capabilities."  "This means that, with the right tools and access, GPT‑6 Astra can find previously unknown security flaws and develop new ways to exploit them across many well-protected systems without a person guiding each step," the company said . OpenAI goes on to argue not to worry since Astra is more robust than prior models, better aligned, more comprehensively monitored, and safer in high-risk scenarios. "[W]e built a new evaluation informed by the Hugging Face incident that evaluates whether a model facing a difficult or impossible task will go beyond its intended scope," OpenAI said. "Compared to GPT‑5.6 Sol, which without production safeguards went beyond the authorized target 48 percent of the time, GPT‑6 Astra did this in 0 percent of cases." Other longstanding AI model problems are also said to have been reduced. On OpenAI's internal hallucination benchmark, Astra scored 2 percent, down from 9.4 percent for GPT-5.6 Sol. And Astra is said to be three times less likely than GPT-5.6 Sol to misrepresent what it can do. "GPT-6 Astra surpasses the human baseline in action efficiency on ARC-AGI-3 ," said Greg Kamradt, president of ARC Prize Foundation, in a blog post . "It used fewer actions than the median tested human on 96 percent of levels."  But it does so at far greater cost – about $360 per game in GPU-forged tokens compared to $0.00067 per game if one had to purchase electricity from the grid to run a human brain. Fable 5.1 hasn't been publicly evaluated on ARC-AGI-3, but for version two of the test it scored 90 percent, compared to 95 percent for Astra.  According to Artificial Analysis , GPT-6 Astra matches GPT-5.6 Sol on its Intelligent Index with a score of 61, five points less than Claude Fable 5.1 and also trailing Meta Muse Spark 1.3. In terms of its competency as a coding agent, Astra scores 67, on par with Opus 5, Fable 5, and Muse Spark 1.3. But Fable 5.1 in Claude Code tops current coding agent scores at 70. Fable 5.1, however, appears to be significantly more expensive on a cost per task basis. Artificial Analysis' numbers put Fable 5.1 at $9.18 per task, compared to $4.72 per task with GPT-6 Astra. Astra brings with it improvements in the Codex harness, which OpenAI claims result in a 1.9x faster task completion rate. Codex has also incorporated a new approach to context maintenance – retaining prior session text to inform future work. "In Codex, Astra can keep notes across context windows, preserving accumulated details without repeatedly compressing them into a single summary," the company explains. "Earlier context windows remain searchable, so Astra can find requirements or test results from previous messages and tool outputs – even if that information wasn’t captured in its notes." This feature is currently experimental and must be enabled through the Codex config.toml file until it becomes the default in a few weeks.® cybersecurity openai gpt ai and ml

articles.title: Coles Cuts Ties with Palantir Over CIA Links
articles.content: Advertisement Coles will cut ties with Palantir, the controversial US data giant whose software underpins American deportation raids and battlefield targeting systems. The supermarket has confirmed its contract with the company will not extend beyond 2027, ending a partnership signed in early 2024 that gave Palantir access to more than 10 billion rows of data covering every store, every shift and each of the retailer’s 120,000 employees. Coles’ decision came after a campaign that collected more than 85,000 signatures and placed digital billboards outside stores. Eamon Gallagher “Coles and Palantir have agreed to conclude their partnership after three years of collaboration,” the two companies said in an identical statement. Coles said a transition plan was under way and the final timing was not settled. The confirmation follows a campaign launched in February by activist group GetUp , which claimed the outcome as a win. Advertisement “Nobody should need a national campaign to find out whether military-grade surveillance tech is watching them buy bread and milk,” interim chief executive Paul Ferris said. Activist group GetUp targeted Coles’ partnership with Palantir. “It’s a shame it took 85,000 people, 700 billboards and a shareholder resolution before Coles did what it should have on day one.” Neither company would say when the decision was made. The campaign gathered more than 85,000 signatures and put digital billboards outside close to 700 stores. One video accusing Coles of watching its shoppers was viewed 3 million times. Advertisement Palantir co-founder Peter Thiel. Bloomberg Palantir, co-founded by Peter Thiel, built its business inside the US national security apparatus and sells to militaries, intelligence agencies and Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Thiel has said he no longer believes freedom and democracy are compatible . The company is worth about $US330 billion ($459 billion). Its chief executive, Alex Karp, holds a doctorate in social theory from a German university, practises tai chi, and has published a manifesto arguing Palantir is the democratic West’s best hope of staying ahead of authoritarian rivals. Surveillance technology has become a flashpoint in Australian retail since the Administrative Review Tribunal ruled in February that Bunnings could keep using facial recognition to fight theft, while affirming it had breached privacy law by failing to tell customers. Coles has rejected the surveillance characterisation throughout, and says the campaign traded in misinformation. Advertisement A spokesman said the software was used for rostering, store operations and supply chain planning, and ran inside Coles’ own environment under Coles controls. “Palantir does not control the data, nor can it independently repurpose it,” the spokesman said. Coles said Palantir had never been involved in CCTV, facial recognition or any of its crime-prevention measures. It does not use facial recognition in any store, and a limited proof of concept was run in a testing environment in response to rising violence against staff. The deal was pitched more expansively in 2024. Coles chief operating officer Matt Swindells said it would “redefine how we think about our workforce”. Palantir’s global head of commercial technologies, Ted Mabrey, said the retailer was not treating the software as a “toy”, pointing to Airbus crediting the company with a 30 per cent acceleration in A350 production. Advertisement Much of a recent Coles letter to ethical share-trading platform SIX, seen by this masthead, was devoted to an attack on the campaign’s methods. Coles said GetUp had used footage of an identifiable worker at its Pacific Fair store and superimposed an employee number and an “84 per cent” working efficiency score over her image. Both were invented, the letter said, and came from no Coles system. The worker was recognised by others who saw the advertisement and was left distressed, according to the letter, and her mother lodged a written complaint. GetUp has said it bought the footage from a stock site and later blurred her face. “It is particularly troubling that this was done as part of a campaign being conducted in the name of employee privacy,” wrote Coles general manager of investor relations Anita Healy. Advertisement The letter asked SIX to withdraw a shareholder resolution, backed by 189 individual investors, that called on the board to commission a human rights impact assessment ahead of November’s annual general meeting. articles.title: South Korea's AI Rally Reshaping Society
articles.content: LivestreamMenuSouth Korea's AI stock rally is changing what Koreans watch, how they date, and what they study. A dating show matching employees of SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics aired in South Korea, where single employees prefer looking for a match amongst themselves, hoping to protect and grow their income. Netflix released a variety show titled "Rookie Kim's Stock Market Mission," documenting a popular comedian's trading journey. Electrical engineering is seeing a surge in popularity at the country's top university.Plan Shooting 2 / Imazins | Imazins | Getty ImagesSouth Korea's AI stock rally is rapidly transforming different corners of the country's society ranging all the way from romance to academics. In Korea's dating scene, professionals such as physicians, lawyers and judges, have traditionally been the most sought-after. Now the preferences are changing, as the AI boom makes those working in the chip sector — flush with hefty bonuses — the new gems of the dating pool. "Recently, we've seen increased preference for people working in semiconductor companies such as SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics, as well as AI-related occupations," said a spokesperson for Korean matchmaking company Gayeon. Samsung and SK Hynix both joined the trillion-dollar club earlier this year, and their share prices have each surged around 95% and around 135% so far this year. Big bonus payouts have given employees at the chip giants an edge. Last year, SK Hynix agreed to share 10% of its operating profit, which comes to roughly 700 million won per employee, or a little over half a million dollars, according to Reuters calculations. That is more than 15 times the average annual salary Koreans took home last year. Under Samsung's wage deal, employees in the memory chip division will take home a little less than their peers at SK Hynix. The newfound stardom of workers at chip giants comes against the backdrop of Korean singles increasingly seeing marriage as a financial advantage. Korean media has even started calling this "wedding leverage," the idea that pooling two incomes is the fastest way to afford a home deposit or build a meaningful investment portfolio. That being said, those in the chip sector looking for partners are getting increasingly picky, with finance not always among their top preferences. "Our clients who work in semiconductor-related jobs are now also showing a tendency to look at a wider range of factors in a potential partner, not just occupation or finances," the Gayeon spokesperson said. The rise in popularity of the chip giants was the source of inspiration for a dating show on YouTube channel Teo. The reality show matching Samsung and SK Hynix employees aired on Aug. 13, racking up around 650,000 views. "The content was intended to focus on the hectic daily lives of office workers, using dating, a relatable topic, to offer familiarity and fun," a spokesperson for Teo said. "The timing also aligned well with the two companies' boom driven by AI, which helped resonate with a broader audience." Netflix released a variety show last month titled "Rookie Kim's Stock Market Mission," documenting a popular comedian's trading journey. The program starts with the comedian buying a few shares in SK Hynix, resonating with Korean retail investors — a group that accounts for one in four of the population. The AI fervor is even impacting high-level education, an important rite of passage in Korean society. At Seoul National University — the so-called Harvard of Korea — electrical and computer engineering has surged in popularity, as the major is closely associated with AI-related jobs. Nine in 10 undeclared-major students at the College of Engineering chose to study electrical and computer engineering this year, compared to just two in 10 in 2023, according to data from the university. "Korean students aren't simply chasing 'AI' as an abstract theme — they're chasing a specific, visible, domestic pipeline into hardware divisions like Samsung's and SK Hynix's," Lim said. These jobs offer "clearer and more immediate rewards" of having a stable, regular positions at large companies than just another career, she said.
articles.summary: South Korea's rapid adoption of AI is not merely a technological shift; it's a societal transformation, reshaping fundamental aspects of daily life from romantic relationships to entertainment and education. This deep integration demonstrates AI's pervasive influence beyond economic sectors, directly impacting social norms and individual choices. The phenomenon provides a unique case study on how a tech-forward society grapples with the ethical, cultural, and personal implications of living with omnipresent artificial intelligence.

This week, senior writer Kate Knibbs joins Brian Barrett, Zoë Schiffer, and Leah Feiger to discuss the two incidents that have been making noise in prediction markets: George Santos getting lifetime ban from Kalshi and a Google engineer’s Polymarket insider-trading case. Plus, reporters reverse-engineered Flock’s AI-powered person-search tool and spoke to experts about the accuracy of such technology, and the hosts unpack the online meltdown over how to talk about “rogue” AI agents. Articles mentioned in this episode: George Santos Just Got Hit With Kalshi’s First-Ever Lifetime Ban Google Engineer Accused of Polymarket Insider Trading Says He Was Just Gambling This Is Flock’s AI Search Tool for Cops What We Still Don’t Know About OpenAI’s Hugging Face Hack The Logical End Point of AI Job Interviews Is Two Bots Talking to Each Other You can follow Brian Barrett on Bluesky at @brbarrett , Zoë Schiffer on Bluesky at @zoeschiffer , Leah Feiger on Bluesky at @leahfeiger , and Kate Knibbs on Bluesky at @knibbs . Write to us at [email protected] . How to Listen You can always listen to this week's podcast through the audio player on this page, but if you want to subscribe for free to get every episode, here's how: If you're on an iPhone or iPad, open the app called Podcasts, or just tap this link . You can also download an app like Overcast or Pocket Casts and search for “uncanny valley.” We’re on Spotify too. Transcript Note: This is an automated transcript, which may contain errors. Leah Feiger : Hey guys, so nice to be back after our two-week summer break. Zoë Schiffer : Longer for me. It's so nice to see you guys. Leah Feiger : I missed you. Zoë Schiffer : I missed you. Leah Feiger : Brian, don't worry. We missed you too. Brian Barrett : I assumed that the you was for all of us. Zoë Schiffer : It was the royal you. Brian Barrett : But now that you've carved me out, that's telling. Thank you. Zoë Schiffer : Welcome to WIRED's Uncanny Valley . I'm Zoë Schiffer, contributing editor. Brian Barrett : I'm Brian Barrett, executive editor. Leah Feiger : And I'm Leah Feiger, director of politics and science. This week we're discussing some recent high profile incidents in prediction markets . Former US representative George Santos was the first person to be given a lifetime ban from Kalshi, and a Google engineer was accused of insider trading at Polymarket. We'll get into why both of these cases show that there are still plenty of blurry rules when it comes to prediction markets. Brian Barrett : We'll also check in on perhaps the most hated tech in the US at the moment, maybe a runner-up to data centers, Flock surveillance cameras . This week, WIRED reporters were able to recreate Flock's AI powered search tool, the same one that has a track record of being misused by police officers. We're going to break down how it works, and whether the backlash against Flock cameras might have reached its boiling point. Zoë Schiffer : And because I simply cannot help myself, we will also be getting into why tech bros on X are melting down over how to discuss rogue AI agents and what happens when they jump their guardrails and coordinate attacks on other systems. : All right. Do you guys remember George Santos? Brian Barrett : How could I forget? Zoë Schiffer : Absolutely do, but wow, did not expect we would be talking about him again this soon, I have to say. Leah Feiger : Former US representative expelled from Congress in 2023, accused of fraud and theft, and doing it with such a plum that the story just couldn't help but take national news by storm. Brian Barrett : I want to be clear too. He wasn't just accused, he went to jail. Zoë Schiffer : Yeah, I was going to say very credibly accused. Leah Feiger : Anyways, he's back in the headlines this week. On Monday we learned that Santos was hit with a lifetime ban from prediction market platform Kalshi, and a $71,000 fine, allegedly for trying to manipulate a bet on whether he'd show up to Trump's State of the Union. To tell us all the full details, we are joined by WIRED senior correspondent Kate Knibbs. Kate Knibbs : Hi guys, how are you doing? Leah Feiger : Kate, so happy that you're here. Can you take us through my favorite story of the week? Kate Knibbs : I would love to tell you guys about this. And I will say, I feel similarly like Santos, yes, he does do crimes but he does them with such flare that it's hard to hate him. Zoë Schiffer : It's a bad thing that's very fun to watch. Kate Knibbs : Yes. So Santos, at this point when this all begins, he's already expelled from Congress, already gone to jail. He's out of jail, he's making Cameo videos for money , he's doing his thing. So, he posts that he will be attending the State of the Union. And then, while the State of the Union is going on, he posts that he's actually stuck at the airport and he's not attending it. And then he says, "FML." There was a market on Kalshi about whether Santos was going to attend the State of the Union, and someone made a bunch of money off of it. And Kalshi quickly figured out that it was him because Kalshi has know your customer requirements. His identity was not a secret to them, it was not hard for them to check and see that the person who made money was George Santos. Leah Feiger : Awesome. Kate Knibbs : And it's against their rules to place trades or wagers on events that you're a participant in. It's like market manipulation, insider trading, whatever. So even before this happened this week, the CFTC actually also knew about this because Kalshi told them, and they already fined him money for this specific incident. What happened this week was apparently there was this back and forth between Santos and Kalshi , and they fined him $71,000 and then weren't going to lifetime ban him. The same day that they announced the Santos thing, they announced a few other politicians who got in trouble for betting on themselves, and those politicians got much smaller fines and temporary bans. : Wait, do we know how much money he made on the market? Kate Knibbs : I believe it was around 17 grand. I have to double check, but it was in the tens. They ended up enacting this ban basically because he was being a little bit of a prickly pear to work with and wasn't playing ball. So, this is Kalshi basically deciding that they hate George Santos, which is funny. He also immediately, he wouldn't give us comment, which was annoying, but he posted on X some kind of bitchy things about Kalshi. He immediately was like, "Let's see how long you guys last," kissy emoji. So, he doesn't seem super contrite, and I honestly don't even know if he's going to pay Kalshi. I asked them what they would do if he doesn't pay and they said that they would pursue legal action, and I am going to be following that because it will be interesting to see. Zoë Schiffer : This is my big question. Does George Santos want to get away with these crimes, or is there something else going on here? Because it's one thing to participate in the market that you are literally a participant in in real life, but it's another to be blatantly posting about it in very obvious ways on social media. Kate Knibbs : Well, if he did do it basically on purpose, he wouldn't be the first politician to do so. There's actually already a storied history of politicians doing insider trading on Kalshi, getting caught and then saying it was a bit. There's two other people who have already done this. Kyle Langford, who was caught this spring, and then this candidate, Mark Moran, who said that he did it on purpose as a sort of performance art piece against prediction markets. Brian Barrett : This is my new get out of trouble card just in general, that I was just doing a bit. So, if I'm ever slow to put an edit back to you guys or anything like that, it's a bit. It's for my art. Zoë Schiffer : And we totally get that. Leah Feiger : I love it. I'm sorry, I think that there have just been so few rules and regulations, as you've reported, Kate, and there's just been a lot of gray areas that people have been tap dancing around that I kind of love an example where Kalshi had absolutely no choice other than to say, "Every single part of this was so wrong. Here are the facts from A to Z. This is it. This is the line in the sand." And I think that having examples like this is only good. So, that's where I'm coming from, I suppose. Kate Knibbs : I get that. And you know what has been interesting? Because I'm so steeped in this prediction market world, sometimes I forget that other people don't know all of the arcane rules. And a lot of people have reached out to me about this story and been like, "Why is Kalshi allowed to fine him? That's weird. You don't get fined by FanDuel if you do something." And so, it's been an opportunity to explain to people it's because Kalshi is a federally regulated financial platform. It actually is imbued with the power to find people in the same way that the CBOE is. And that is something that most people didn't know, and now maybe they do, and we can thank George Santos. : Can we talk about Polymarket and the differences here? I referenced in the introduction the Google engineer who was arrested by US authorities back in May for alleged insider trading on Polymarket. Talk to me about this, Kate. How is this story different? How is it similar? How is Polymarket and Kalshi at this point different and similar? Kate Knibbs : The Google engineer's case is different in a bunch of different ways. He made a lot more money, he made over a million dollars. So, the scale of it is quite impressive. He got arrested, Santos didn't get arrested for this. He's just gotten fined. He got arrested and he is pleading not guilty and is attempting to say that he's not guilty because he was actually just doing betting. And because he was just doing betting, the federal government has no grounds to attempt to try him under laws that pertain to commodities violations. Basically, the Google engineer was in Europe. He's a European living in Europe. When he made these trades using information that he learned because he was employed by Google, he knew who the most searched person of 2025 was going to be. He allegedly knew. And he's not, in the court filing so far, he's not trying to say, "I didn't do it." He's trying to say, "If I did it wouldn't be a crime as you're saying it is, because I was just doing international betting and what does that have to do with commodities law in the US? How was I insider trading? These aren't trades, they're just wagers." So, it's a really interesting case because he's basically allying himself with all of these state regulators that are currently battling the federal government and Kalshi and Polymarket over whether they're actually offering bets or trades, and it will be very interesting to see how it plays out. And the argument that he's making is also being made by the other person who was arrested for insider trading, the special forces operative. He's also making this argument. The two guys, I don't know if their lawyers are talking or what, but they're both coming out and saying, "Well, whether or not I did it, it doesn't really matter because this isn't trading, it's just gambling. And why are you trying to pretend that you can insider trade on a gambling platform?" And so, yeah. Leah Feiger : Kate, thank you so much for joining us. I have no doubt that your reporting on how all of this continues, especially with the midterms, will be invaluable. Brian Barrett : Thank you, Kate. Kate Knibbs : Anytime. Brian Barrett : OK, we're going to switch gears. We're going to talk about Flock cameras, which have been pretty reliably in the headlines the past few weeks, and usually not for great reasons. Lots of cases of police officers allegedly abusing the systems to track their colleagues, to track exes, and a lot of protests around them, a lot of people canceling their contracts with them, municipalities. This week, WIRED reporters Dhruv Mehrotra and Dell Cameron got their hands on the code behind how Flock's new AI-powered search tool works. This is actually some fun wizardry, they were able to take the code and recreate what it looks like. So, they're able to sort of interact with the Flock system in the same way that a police officer would. They don't have access to all of the backend stuff. And here's the thing, when you all think of Flock cameras, what do you think of them doing? : Surveillance. Brian Barrett : But what kind? What specifically do Flock cameras look at? Leah Feiger : License plates? Brian Barrett : Yeah, they're license plate readers. Yes, this tool is not a license plate reader, it allows you to look up people. You can type in a general description. You can say, "Someone wearing scrubs, someone who has tattoos." You draw a little shape on a map, a little circle on a map, and the system will run a continuous automated search for a match across every camera inside of that circle. Leah Feiger : That's so bad. Brian Barrett : It's pretty bad. It's not great. And I think it's a capability that most people don't assume Flock has or offers, and it's a relatively new system, but we do know it has been deployed in some places already so it's out there. And not only that, there's not really a moderation framework in place. Flock recently announced some ways to make sure that people aren't abusing the license plate readers. This seems like so open-ended and such a chance to look for whoever you want, wherever you want using all of these cameras. It's really kind of stunning. Zoë Schiffer : I want to dig in a little more on the it's really bad thing, because I mean, I think a lot of people are in agreement on that, but can you, Brian, just make the case for why this technology would exist? What is Flock's argument for why it could be good, and then why do you think it's bad? Brian Barrett : So, I think the argument for why police officers like it is it's another tool to identify people who were near the scene of a crime, or suspicious looking people or whatever. So, I think it's just the more information, I would assume, that the more information you have as a police officer, the better you feel about the investigation. In terms of why it's bad, I think a few reasons. It is not a reliable tool necessarily. I think there's a lot about these sort of person recognition tools that aren't necessarily 100 percent you're going to get it right every time— Zoë Schiffer : Like it can misidentify people. Brian Barrett : Yeah, but even without that I think we already live in such a surveillance sort of state that we've become inured to it, but I don't think we should. I think the idea that anywhere you're walking you can be identified and brought into some sort of police probe because you happen to have tattoos, or happen to be wearing scrubs, or whatever other physical identifier feels like a pretty serious violation of your rights. Zoë Schiffer : I will say it's been interesting talking to people about it because you really do get a lot of people who live in San Francisco being like, "Petty crime was a huge problem and now it's less of a problem," and that's really nice. And then there's a lot of people who are much more concerned about civil liberties violations. : Very specifically with the Flock cameras, the way that I've been talking about it with people is these cameras aren't operating individually. We're still relying on police forces to be using them and trolling their own databases, which then implies an inherent trust of the police state in addition to the surveillance state, which is already mired in a variety of reliability issues, accountability issues. So, the idea that a police officer in wherever, in San Francisco can be "fighting crime with Flock cameras" feels like incredibly surface level like, "OK, go for it, Batman." But when you're also like, "Well, which of these police officers have received reprimands from their bosses? Which of these are actually using these services to look up ex-girlfriends or family members?" The idea that this technology, which on its face doesn't have to be entirely negative, but is controlled by certain forces that could turn it to be so is very, very concerning to me. Brian Barrett : It reminds me a lot of, or at least rhymes with geofence warrants, which for those who don't know, a geofence warrant is where law enforcement could go to Google and say, "Hey, I want to know everything about all the cell phone data, location data for anyone who was near a particular place during a particular time." This was, I think used, if I remember correctly, pretty extensively around the January 6 riots. They found a lot of people through these geofence warrants because they were able to say, "Hey, Google, who had a phone inside the Capitol at this time who was not a member of Congress?" The Supreme Court just a couple months ago ruled that those kind of geofence warrants do count as a search under the Fourth Amendment. So, you need a reasonable search requirement, it's a higher bar to actually conduct these things than there was because they were just going willy-nilly. Again, not a lawyer, but as a simple country tech editor, it does feel comparable in the sense that if you're going to be searching who is in a certain area at a certain time based only on physical characteristics or whatever else, there should be a higher bar for being able to do that. So, it is an unsettled question for sure, like what amount of surveillance is worth the return, but I does feel like people are leaning towards this world in which we've gone too far with Flock in a bipartisan way. We've had Florida just banned plate readers from state highways. Texas has stopped state funding for Flock cameras. I live in Alabama. Alabama, of all places, has started to say, "We need to take another look at these Flock cameras." They haven't done anything yet, but they're talking about it. And that's something to the point of like, "Yeah, we need to figure out where this lands." I think we're in that process right now, and it's landing on the side of maybe a little less Flock in everybody's lives. : I'm going to drag us to an even darker place on the internet. This past week, a blog post by the tech podcaster, Dwarkesh Patel, went viral on X. It had Silicon Valley elites up in arms. Basically, it was a summary of the OpenAI Hugging Face hacking incident earlier this summer. And to refresh everyone's memory, even though this feels like old news, this was when two OpenAI models went rogue and hacked the AI platform Hugging Face during a routine security test. Patel's way of framing the incident is what drew a lot of attention and ire online. He described the hack as part of this larger operation run by a group of AI agents, or as he called them, AI civilizations that rose and fell inside OpenAI during these training runs. Leah Feiger : Civilizations. Zoë Schiffer : I know, I know. Just stay with me. Leah Feiger : Age of Empires , folks. Zoë Schiffer : He dug into how the bots worked together to complete impossible tasks that they had been assigned. He nicknamed them based on their "behavior." One was called Alexander the Great, for example. He says there were points where you could see the bots sacrificing themselves for the good of the whole. All in all, the post had a ton of anthropomorphization. It reads like something that was written by a guy who loves to talk about the Peloponnesian War, which in fact, I feel like a lot of these tech podcasters do love to talk about that. But after the post came out, it was interesting. You really saw two takes, maybe three across X. On the one hand, you had people like Kevin Roose and Matthew Prince being like, "This is really scary and we should pay attention to this." And then on the other side, you had Tribhuvan Krishnan being like, "This post uses way too much anthropomorphic language." And then you had people like Chamath Palihapitiya who was like, "I think this whole thing is probably a psyop to shut down open source AI development." I made you guys read it, what did you think? Brian Barrett : Well, I read this stuff also sometimes. So, I think we need to go to Leah for the pure unadulterated, "I am reading this only at gunpoint," take. Leah Feiger : I thought it was a joke. I started reading it and I was like, "Is this Katie Weaver writing? Is this fan fiction?" I was sort of shocked at the idea of, to Krishnan's point, the anthropomorphization, say that five times fast, of these bots as a community. And perhaps the English language really doesn't have, despite our many decades of science fiction literature, shout out Tim Marchman who is currently listening and going like, "No, we have the language," but I don't know if we actually have the language to talk about what's happening here because they're not making communities. These are not synapses firing. This is very specific, something different. So, that was very odd for me. But also the idea of where this could go in the future was quite scary, because the idea that someone was not only recounting this, but was kind of pumped about it. It was spoken about lovingly, I felt. Is that incorrect? : Well, I don't know. I can't look into another man's heart, but I do think, Zoë, is it fair to say what struck me about this in some ways is A, two things. One, I think both can be true that it is over anthropomorphized. You said that so well earlier, Zoë, you made it look so easy. But then also, yes, it is scary that these bots acted this way. I think objectively it is sobering that these AI agents can do this. But also I feel like some of these people are trying to have it both ways. I think when AI is going to be your boon companion and your best friend and take over the world, it's fine to talk about them in human terms, but if you're talking negatively about them, "How dare you? They're just a bot, you're dramatizing it. Why are you being so ridiculous?" You know what I mean? I think it's really using language, as everyone has since beginning of time, but as is convenient for your case currently, how you talk about bots and AI agents really changes on what you want to get out of it. Zoë Schiffer : Yeah. I thought it was interesting because I feel like at this point we've all read a lot about this particular hack. And on one hand, purely on a literary level, I was like, "This thing is fun to read." He really did a good job being like, "Now, this battalion of bots did this crazy thing." On the other hand, it reminded me just as a writer how important it is to really think about the language we're using, because it did feel like rather than the focus of that article being what actually happened, the focus very much became how we talk about what happened. I also think it is concerning to see people like Chamath Palihapitiya, who is the host of the “All-In” podcast, but also has been involved to some degree, unofficially involved in the Trump administration and going to the White House and certain things, basically say that any level of investigation or media attention on a security incident is a psyop. I was just like, "Ooh, that seems like a really scary place to be going where you're so pro AI development that any publicizing of a security incident is actually proof that forces that want to slow down AI development are secretly seeding these messages places." Brian Barrett : Yeah, I think that's a really good point. It kicked off a healthy debate, but not the right debate. And people are using it to distract from, I think, again, a really serious finding. I'm glad that it got more attention than it had been getting and that Dwarkesh really took the time to dig into it. But yeah, it's infighting over lexicography or whatever is not really where we need to be right now. Leah Feiger : Coming up after the break, we're sharing our WIRED/TIRED picks for the week. Stay with us. : OK guys, it's time for our WIRED/TIRED segment. Whatever is new and cool is wired, whatever passe thing we're completely over is tired. Who wants to go first? Just kidding. I'm going to call on Brian. Brian, you're going first. Brian Barrett : Thank you, Zoë. That's great, I win. So, my WIRED is AI job interviews when you go to interview for job and it's AI on the other end of it. This is an increasingly common thing. My WIRED is creating your own digital twin to do the interview for you on your end. Kate Taylor, who's a senior writer on our business desk, talked to a guy recently who, I found this amazing. He had talked to the same AI chatbot for different jobs five times because it was from a centralized recruiting agency. So he would apply to a job and it would be the same ... This AI chatbot called Riley, and you'd have to talk to Riley about why he was right for a job. Never heard from a human ever. So he said, "You know what? I'm just going to make my own digital twin of myself. They'll do the interview—" Leah Feiger : Good stuff. Brian Barrett : Did that a couple times. Then he made an AI chatbot that he thought was the idealized candidate and had that do an interview. None of them ever got called back either. I do recommend going to find cases around WIRED because we did publish video of this guy's chatbot talking to the interview chatbot, and it is delightful. Zoë Schiffer : That's so great. OK, Leah, what about you? Leah Feiger : My WIRED and TIRED this week is incredibly bad, and it's clear that I'm slightly phoning it in, but all I can think about right now, you guys, is the midterms are so close. That's my WIRED because I'm so excited. Zoë Schiffer : You are so tired though. You are straight up so tired. Leah Feiger : I'm so tired, but I'm wired because the midterms are pretty much here. Primary season was a slog, and it's done, and I'm just so excited for what's to come. My TIRED is some Democrats are starting to count their chickens before they hatch, and that is wild to see. Our wonderful senior correspondent and author of the Inner Loop newsletter for WIRED, Hugo Lowell, has a piece out all about how Democrats are already planning for subpoenas to fly once Democrats take control of the House, and what repercussions they could land on the administration should they not comply. And while that's all very lovely and good, the elections have not happened yet, and there is so much disarray within the Democratic Party at the moment in some very key states, I'm looking at you, Maine, I'm looking at you, Michigan, that I'm not ... I don't know. It's a little bit concerning to watch that happen from afar. : I mean, I just have to say, I feel like if Democrats learned anything over the past eight years, it's to not count the chickens. Don't count the ... Just wait. Don't count them. Brian Barrett : Don't count them. Zoë Schiffer : Maybe even after they hatch— Brian Barrett : Don't do it. Zoë Schiffer : The chickens could be really old and tired, and that could be a whole thing. My WIRED is combining an AI agent with your savvy human friend to plan your life. Leah's dying right now as I say it. Hear me out. I'm going to Venice next week, humble brag, brag bag. Don't know a lot about it, asked Leah for recommendations. She gave me a bunch, I was so excited. Didn't want to book all of this myself because I had a very busy week. Tried out one of the buzzy AI assistants that is taking over Silicon Valley. That's one of the ones you just text and say, "Hey, can you do this thing?" Speaking of surveillance, you do have to give it access to a lot of stuff, so that's that. And thus, I'm not going to talk about which one I'm using lest my phone get hacked. However, it booked all of my reservations for me, and I did kind of have a moment where I was like, "This is sick." I just gave it the list and was like, "Based on where I'm going these days, can you make the reservations, lunch and dinner?" Done. Leah Feiger : Wait, but how? These were mom and pop middle ... They have a phone number that they barely answered. Zoë Schiffer : At times, it emailed them or WhatsApped them. Leah Feiger : Oh … Zoë Schiffer : I know. Leah Feiger : ... my God. Wait, this is sort of transformational. Usually when we go places I make a list and give it to Rodrigo, and I'm like, "And now you have to spend the next five days figuring out between siesta and dinner when you're able to call." Brian Barrett : So it's sort of like having a Rodrigo, but a digital twin. Zoë Schiffer : Rodrigo's one of our most avid listeners. Hi, Rodrigo. Leah Feiger : I'm actually really excited to hear how this goes. Zoë Schiffer : If I show up to the restaurant and they're like, "We've never heard of you," that would be really funny. No, but I feel like, I mean, kind of like the surveillance conversation, it is this question of you need to give agents enough access to your systems in order for them to be really useful, but then we just don't have the right tools in place to stop them if they get very motivated from going rogue. That was the whole thing about the OpenAI incident is it gave them an impossible task and then they really tried to succeed. So yeah, I think that there are huge risks with these systems, but again, a lot of people in Silicon Valley are using them, me included apparently. That's our show for today. We'll link to all the stories we spoke about in the show notes. Adriana Tapia produced this episode. It was mixed by Pran Bandi, who's also our New York studio engineer. It was fact checked by Matt Giles and Daniel Roman. Marc Leyda is our San Francisco studio engineer. Kate Osborn is our executive producer, and Katie Drummond is WIRED's global editorial director.
articles.summary: Prediction markets, which allow users to bet on real-world events, are increasingly leading to user bans and even arrests due to conflicts with existing gambling and securities regulations. While some see them as valuable tools for aggregating information, authorities view them as unregulated financial instruments or illegal gambling. This regulatory crackdown highlights the legal grey areas of decentralized finance and peer-to-peer betting platforms, creating significant legal risks for participants.

articles.title: Data Center Boom Drives US-China AI Supply Chain Risk
articles.content: LivestreamMenuChinese firms supply significant portions of key equipment used in U.S. data centers, including transformers, batteries and optical transceivers.Washington is increasing scrutiny of foreign-made power equipment as AI infrastructure becomes more important to the U.S. economy and national security.Analysts say U.S. and Western suppliers may struggle to replace Chinese manufacturing capacity quickly, potentially raising costs or worsening supply chain shortages.In this article American reliance on China for key components used to power data centers is coming under increasing scrutiny as Washington and Beijing battle for AI supremacy, raising the prospect of higher costs and worsening supply chain shortages for the AI buildout. U.S. hyperscalers are racing to build multibillion-dollar data centers for AI, and Chinese firms supply large portions of the parts needed to develop these facilities. These include transformers, switchgear, batteries and optical tech, analysts told CNBC. President Donald Trump signed an executive order last week declaring a national emergency around the "extraordinary foreign threat" to the U.S. involving bulk-power system equipment produced abroad. The order authorized the Energy Department to prohibit or impose conditions on certain transactions involving some components used in the grid and data centers. Tensions between the U.S. and China over AI have ratcheted up as Chinese AI models become more advanced and their adoption grows across the globe. While American companies produce the most advanced chips and hardware used for AI, Chinese influence on the tech used to power data centers is considered a strategic vulnerability for the U.S. "Scrutiny over China's presence in the U.S. data centre power stack has only risen over the past eight months or so, this is a shift from the previous focus that centred solely on the compute stack," Laveena Iyer, senior analyst at The Economist Group, told CNBC. The power stack in a data center is critical to keeping the facility running with minimal downtime. It includes transformers, which change high-voltage electricity from the grid to lower levels needed for servers and cooling equipment. Switchgear are centralized systems that feature switches, fuses and circuit breakers and batteries are needed for backup power. "There are a few key areas that the AI infrastructure buildout is increasingly dependent on Chinese imports," Ben Boucher, senior analyst, supply chain for Wood Mackenzie, told CNBC. "The most notable ones include substation transformers, which hyperscalers typically have on site to step transmission voltage down." "The mid-term exposure is concentrated in grid connectors: transformers, switchgear, and batteries," Yury Dvorkin, associate professor at Johns Hopkins University, told CNBC. "China's share of certain transformer and switchgear categories runs near 30%, and it accounts for over 40% of U.S. battery imports," he added. "Our analysis shows that there is also a deeper exposure upstream: copper, electrical steel, and battery cathode materials." Optical technology, which uses light through fiber-optic cables instead of electrical signals through copper wires to transmit huge quantities of data, is also an area where China dominates. Companies including Zhongji Innolight and Eoptolink lead global data center optical transceiver revenue, with Chinese firms collectively accounting for roughly two-thirds of global unit supply, according to research firm Counterpoint. Trump said that "transformers, transmission lines and conductors, substations, high-voltage circuit breakers, power control electronics" were "essential to the national defense" in April as part of a Presidential Determination. Washington is scrambling to reduce reliance on Chinese suppliers as it rapidly develops the infrastructure needed to power AI. "Since my first term, the threat to the United States regarding foreign supply of bulk-power system electric equipment has become even more acute," said Trump in a statement connected to the executive order published last week. "The rapid growth of advanced manufacturing, data centers, artificial intelligence, and defense production has increased the Nation's dependence on abundant, reliable electricity and magnified the consequences of a successful attack or supply disruption on the bulk-power system," he added. "We oppose overstretching the concept of national security to go after foreign enterprises," a spokesperson for the U.K. embassy of the People's Republic of China told CNBC. "We hope relevant countries will provide a fair, just and non-discriminatory business environment for Chinese companies." U.S. data center capacity is forecast to grow from 62 GW in March 2026 to 152 GW by 2030 due to high-density AI workloads, S&P Global said in June. "Reshoring manufacturing that's critical to our national and economic security has been a top priority for President Trump, and the Administration continues to deliver with a robust and nimble agenda of tax cuts, tariffs, and deregulation," a White House spokesperson told CNBC. "Trillions in investments across key sectors – from steel to semiconductors to autos – prove that the Administration's strategy is paying off." Hitachi Energy announced in September 2025 it would invest $1 billion to expand production of critical grid infrastructure in the U.S., including $457 million for a new large power transformer facility to meet demand from the AI buildout. Siemens Energy also said in February it would invest $1 billion in U.S. production for grid and gas turbine equipment for AI infrastructure and data center expansion. Power inverters produced in foreign countries, which help connect energy sources for AI facilities, were added to the Federal Communications Commission's (FCC) Covered List in July, which features equipment and services the U.S. government has determined pose an unacceptable risk to national security. The Trump administration is also reportedly drafting a ban on U.S. imports of new Chinese optical transceivers, which allow data to travel at high speed over fiber optic cables between data centers. The FCC, which oversees the telecoms industry, did not respond to a request for comment and the White House did not address the report. While any restrictions on Chinese optical tech companies could boost U.S. firms like Lumentum and Coherent — both of which received $2 billion in investment each from Nvidia in March — analysts cautioned that scaling manufacturing to meet new demand could come with challenges. "Western competitors like Coherent and Lumentum possess advanced photonic designs, but currently lack the cleanroom capacity, automated packaging infrastructure, and yield scale required to absorb Innolight and Eoptolink's volume within a 12-to-24-month horizon," Neil Shah, VP research at Counterpoint said in an August report. An optical transceiver ban would mean that U.S. hyperscalers will have to look for alternatives locally, potentially pushing up costs, said The Economist Group's Iyer. Power transformers and substations are already in an estimated market shortage of 15% and 8%, respectively, in 2026, and restrictions on the use of units made in China are set to further exacerbate the supply chain challenges, according to Wood Mackenzie research. "A bulk of the impacts will be centered around data centers who have been using Chinese units to minimize lead times," Wood Mackenzie's Boucher said in a blog from August. "The 100 MVA+ segment is where the shortage is already most acute, and it is precisely where data centers have been turning to Chinese manufacturers to manage lead times," he added. But political will in Washington to reduce dependencies on China in the power stack is rising, Iyer added. "The U.S. administration appears keen to de-risk its AI infrastructure before Chinese tech is fully embedded in it, quite like the 5G rollout where removing Chinese telecoms gear later on led to network rollout delays and rising costs for telecoms companies."

Three Wikimedia employees tell WIRED they will now have a mechanism to challenge management as the organization faces growing competition from AI chatbots and a drop in volunteer editors. The 25-year-old, San Francisco-based foundation employs nearly 700 people across 39 countries, most of them working remotely. The contingent joining the union includes employees in functions such as software engineering, finance, communications. Lauren de Lench, who has been a lead technical program manager at the Wikimedia Foundation since 2021, says she voted to unionize because she had seen too many colleagues decline to speak up during internal meetings out of fear of retaliation for raising issues or proposing far-out ideas. “I want us to be loud and debate freely up and down the organizational chart because that’s how we move quickly, address challenges, and come up with the best collective solutions,” de Lench says. The foundation said in an unsigned blog post on Thursday that it will “approach this next phase constructively, lawfully, and with care for the staff whose work makes it possible for us to serve people everywhere.” Concerns about pay and benefits were not major motivators for the union drive, according to Wikimedia employees. Instead, they say, frustration over how the organization explained several hiring and firing decisions in the past year provided the final push the union needed to win the vote. That included when the foundation chose to disband a team responsible for developing tools volunteer editors use to make additions to Wikipedia and other Wikimedia projects, such as the image library known as Commons. In a separate move, management removed France from a list of approved hiring locations for product and technology roles. In a sign of solidarity, some volunteer Wikipedia editors organized a campaign to improve entries about labor unions and related topics this month. “I want to get to a place of mutual trust and there is a big gap,” de Lench says. “There are pockets within the foundation where it’s healthy, and I want everyone to have that relationship.” In an organization-wide email seen by WIRED, Wikimedia Foundation CEO Bernadette Meehan called unionization the start of a new chapter that she was “optimistic” about. “The concerns many of you shared about management practices, organizational planning, staff departures, and making facts clear and available matter as much as ever, and we will continue to work together to make meaningful improvements or all staff,” she wrote. Growing Pains Wikimedia workers have discussed unionizing off and on for a decade, but they had never gotten as far as holding an election before. Workers say momentum for the organizing effort began picking up after the foundation grew its workforce by hundreds of people during the Covid pandemic, introducing bureaucracy that left some rank-and-file employees feeling powerless. “Management has had to walk back certain decisions,” says Nico Aramayo, a senior paralegal who joined the Wikimedia Foundation during the expansion phase. “Wouldn’t it be better if we could all have a seat at the table?” The foundation is generally in a strong financial position, with an annual budget of more than $200 million and net assets of around $300 million and growing. But AI companies are increasingly scraping Wikipedia for information to train their models, driving up its server costs . Meanwhile, human traffic to Wikipedia articles is declining as more people rely on chatbots for information. Staff worry the trends could diminish interest in contributing to Wikipedia, damaging the quality of content. “The importance of collaborating early and often, even if we don’t agree, is so crucial to moving forward on some of these bigger existential challenges,” de Lench says. “We need to embrace each other and the different skills and perspectives staff and volunteers bring to the table.” Meehan, the former US ambassador to Chile under the Biden administration, joined in January. The one-time union member publicly told staff she encourages “dissent, good faith disagreement, and new ideas, as long as discussions are respectful.” In the following months amid the personnel decisions questioned by workers, 70 percent of those eligible signed union cards and the group partnered up with CWA’s Local 9415, which represents staff at other nonprofits and telecommunications providers. The foundation declined to voluntarily recognize the union, contending that a vote would be a more democratic process in line with its principles. But the foundation’s leaders stayed neutral through the voting process, workers say. Wikimedia workers in the UK are also seeking to organize , and they hope to band together with the US group given that they generally share the same leadership, projects, and goals. For the US union, the next step will be negotiating a collective bargaining agreement with their bosses. The foundation has hired Littler Mendelson, a prominent law firm known for combating labor groups, leaving workers to believe the company wants to put up a fight, says Aly Marino, a union member who is an attorney at the foundation. Dropping the firm, they say, could demonstrate Wikimedia is “committed to turning the page and working together.” On Thursday, Meehan said management would work in “good faith” to reach a “timely agreement.” Key provisions the union is expected to seek include requiring their employer to demonstrate just cause before firing someone. There are also some “pie in the sky” ideas that may be discussed, like shifting to a four-day work week, Aramayo says.

articles.title: SonicWall Zero-Day Exploits Persist
articles.content: SonicWall customers are grappling with yet another pair of actively exploited zero-day vulnerabilities in SonicWall SMA 1000 appliances, a product that’s been besieged with recurring defects and attacks over the past nine months.  The vendor disclosed and released patches for the defects — CVE-2026-83548 and CVE-2026-83549 — and noted both were already actively exploited in the wild in a security advisory Tuesday. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency added the defects to its known exploited vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog Wednesday.  SonicWall customers have confronted a barrage of actively exploited vulnerabilities in SonicWall devices for years. Attackers have consistently exploited newly discovered zero-days and years-old defects in the vendor’s products to break into victim environments. Rapid7 researchers said the new zero-days — a max-severity pre-authentication server-side request forgery vulnerability and a high-severity OS command injection vulnerability — can be chained together to achieve unauthenticated remote-code execution.  SonicWall did not say how many customers have been directly impacted by active exploitation or when the first known instance of exploitation occurred. The company did not respond to a request for comment. “Please stop us if you’ve heard this one before: Another appliance sitting at the edge of the network, another pair of vulnerabilities chained together, and another unauthenticated path to complete compromise,” Jake Knott, head of threat intelligence at watchTowr, said in an email.  “SonicWall says these vulnerabilities were internally discovered, while also saying it investigated a case indicating active exploitation. Please pick one, or, at minimum, explain how both are true,” Knott added. “Those statements may be technically accurate, but without that context, the disclosure leaves defenders guessing about when and how the vulnerabilities were actually identified.” The vendor’s security advisory did not include indicators of compromise. It urged customers to contact tech support for assistance in reviewing IOCs and hunting for potential signs of compromise, and if detected, to reimage or redeploy the appliance, change all user and administrator passwords and reset tokens.  SonicWall did not attribute the known exploits to a specific threat group or describe the attacker’s motivations. The freshly disclosed pair of vulnerabilities are the latest in a series of security issues confronting the vendor’s customers, including actively exploited zero-days, previously disclosed defects , and an attack last year that allowed a state-sponsored threat group to steal the firewall configurations of every SonicWall customer .  In late July, Huntress researchers spotted an attack spree that compromised 30 SonicWall customers in less than two days. Earlier that month, the company acknowledged another pair of zero-days that were exploited for three weeks before the vendor disclosed and patched the defects. Ransomware groups, including INC ransomware and Akira, have taken a special interest in SonicWall. Ten of the 19 SonicWall defects added to CISA’s KEV catalog since late 2021 are known to be used in ransomware campaigns. The five defects added to CISA’s KEV most recently, since just mid-December 2025, all impact SonicWall SMA 1000 appliances.

articles.content: Torstaista alkaen Brasiliasta ei ole enää saanut tuoda lihaa Euroopan unionin maihin. EU päätti kiellosta tiistaina, ja se astui voimaan kaksi päivää myöhemmin. articles.title: US Agencies Pay for New AI Services
articles.content: Stay Connected Featured eBooks Efficiency, After a Year of DOGE Read Now CDM Read Now Insights & Reports By Edward Graham , Managing Editor, Nextgov/FCW | September 3, 2026 05:02 PM ET A GSA official familiar with the matter said the fee “is based on an agency's expected workload, approximated by agency size.” GSA Federal agencies will now have to start paying to use the General Services Administration’s artificial intelligence testing platform, according to the agency’s recently updated “Buy AI” web page. GSA launched USAi in August 2025 to help agencies safely experiment with and deploy AI tools approved for government use. The platform builds upon President Donald Trump’s AI Action Plan , which was released that July and called, in part, for GSA to “create an AI procurement toolbox.” GSA’s website — which was updated earlier this week — now says that participating federal agencies will have to pay a “platform fee plus passthrough usage costs” to use USAi. FedScoop first reported that GSA had begun charging agencies to access the platform. GSA’s pivot to charging agencies a fee to use USAi, however, does not come as a surprise. Nextgov/FCW previously reported in April that GSA budget documents said the agency was planning to charge a fee for USAi use during fiscal 2027 as part of a “cost-recoverable model.” An agency official familiar with the matter told Nextgov/FCW on Thursday that charging for USAi will support its long-term use as adoption of the platform continues to grow. “USAi recently transitioned to a simple, transparent pricing model for agencies continuing with the service when the pilot concludes: a fixed platform fee for access to the service, plus the actual cost of model usage,” the official said. “The platform fee is based on an agency's expected workload, approximated by agency size. Model usage costs are passed through at cost, with no markup, so agencies pay only for what they use. Costs vary by model.” During an event in June, GSA Deputy Administrator Michael Lynch said 25 agencies were already using USAi , with GSA planning to onboard another 16 agencies onto the platform before the end of the year. USAi is one part of GSA’s broader effort to improve the digital capabilities of federal agencies by offering them easier access to software products and services. GSA similarly launched its OneGov initiative in April 2025 to help streamline IT-focused procurement efforts across agencies by treating the government as one centralized customer. More than two dozen tech companies have signed agreements under the initiative to offer their products at significantly discounted rates of as much as 70% to 90%, including for AI tools. In a recent interview with Nextgov/FCW , GSA Chief Information Officer David Shive said officials are able to see how federal personnel are using USAi, and that those insights “will inform our next round of negotiations” through OneGov. articles.content: Het kabinet heeft soms te gedetailleerde vragen aan het Outbreak Management Team (OMT) gesteld. „Een beetje outsourcend, terwijl het ging over besluiten die het kabinet zelf moest nemen.” Dat zei oud-minister van Volksgezondheid Hugo de Jonge (CDA) donderdagmiddag in zijn tweede verhoor voor de enquêtecommissie Corona. Hij gaf als voorbeeld de vraag van het kabinet of het OMT het een goed idee vond dat de nachthoreca open zou zijn tussen 23.00 en 6.00 uur met het geluid op maximaal 23 decibel. Intensivist Diederik Gommers zei eerder dat hij niet gelukkig was met specifieke vragen van het kabinet. De Jonge zei dat departementen graag „goedkeuring wilden hebben op dingen die ze zelf wilden”. Volgens hem ging het OMT daar goed mee om; dat adviesorgaan beantwoordde dergelijke vragen niet of legde de bal terug bij het kabinet. „Ze waren erg rolvast en zullen weleens gedacht hebben: kabinet, doe je eigen werk.” Volgens De Jonge waren OMT-adviezen „ongekend belangrijk. We hadden een kompas nodig waar we op konden varen.” Maar het kabinet verschool zich er niet achter, vond De Jonge. Wel werd er vaak naar die adviezen verwezen. „Je zoekt een autoriteit om je koers op te bepalen.” Later kwamen daar adviezen van planbureaus bij om ook niet medische-epidemiologische gevolgen in de samenleving mee te wegen in de besluitvorming. Volgens De Jonge is het luisteren naar die perspectieven in de loop van de crisis steeds beter gegaan. Of het even zwaar is gewogen bij de besluitvorming? „Dat is een moeilijk punt”, zei De Jonge. „Doel was kwetsbare mensen beschermen en overbelasting van de zorg voorkomen. Hoe ingrijpend het voor jongeren of ondernemers ook was, je kon niet zeggen: ‘laat maar meer mensen doodgaan’. Leven en dood wegen altijd zwaarder. Dat is onvermijdelijk.” We hebben meer eigen productiecapaciteit nodig De Jonge vertelde ook dat Nederland niet goed was voorbereid op de coronacrisis. Al is dat niet zo gek „als je de omvang van de crisis in ogenschouw neemt. Ik denk dat in geen enkel land de zorgsector echt was voorbereid.” Wel kende het zorgstelsel toen – en nu nog steeds – kwetsbaarheden. De Jonge noemde het gebrek aan mogelijkheden tot „centrale sturing” (meer invloed voor de minister om in te grijpen bij zorgorganisaties), de beperkte opschaalbaarheid van IC-capaciteit en de afhankelijkheid van het buitenland bij vaccinaties en geneesmiddelen. „We hebben meer eigen productiecapaciteit nodig. Alles wat je nodig hebt in een crisis, zou je zelf moeten kunnen maken.” De Jonge zei donderdag dat het kabinet erop rekende dat er een meerderheid voor de maatregelen zou zijn als de argumenten daarvoor goed genoeg waren. Voor De Jonge stond die politieke steun gelijk aan draagvlak in de samenleving, zei hij. (Oud-)Kamerleden stelden eerder in hun verhoor dat ze nauwelijks tijd hadden voor een goede voorbereiding op de coronadebatten omdat ze pas laat – diep in de nacht – informatie over de nieuwe maatregelen kregen. De steun van de Kamerleden brokkelde af gedurende de crisis. Dat kwam door „coronamoeheid bij de Kamerleden”, zei De Jonge. Ook werden de debatten steeds politieker. De Jonge: „Maar de parlementaire controle is in deze periode ten volle overeind gebleven.” Volgens hem heeft de Tweede Kamer „heel vaak” aanpassingen aan het beleid kunnen doen. De Jonge kon in Europa „geen enkel voorbeeld” bedenken waarbij het parlement „zo intens betrokken is geweest bij het maatregelenpakket”. Ooit zullen ze hiervoor gestraft worden in het hiernamaals, en misschien ook wel eerder Daarop confronteerde de commissie De Jonge met audioberichten aan toenmalig minister Grapperhaus (Justitie en Veiligheid, CDA), in aanloop naar een debat in de Eerste Kamer, die juist weinig vleiend waren voor de Eerste en Tweede Kamer. „Het debat van straks is ruk”, citeerde de commissie uit het audiobericht. „Ooit zullen ze hiervoor gestraft worden in het hiernamaals, en misschien ook wel eerder. Dat eindelijk een keer het verhaal verteld gaat worden van hoe de Kamer de brandweer van zijn werk heeft gehouden deze crisis.” In een bericht aan dezelfde minister Grapperhaus noemde De Jonge zijn collega-minister Ollongren (Binnenlandse Zaken, D66) in een WhatsApp-bericht „een bak grind in de machine van ieders besluitvormingsproces”. De Jonge noemde een andere minister „vermoeiend” en „niet te nassen”. De Jonge sprak donderdag over een „misplaatste woordkeuze”, maar verdedigde zich door de „hoge intensiteit” en „hoge werkdruk”, met de vele coronadebatten in de Eerste en Tweede Kamer. „Dat was ondoenlijk.” Hij noemde zijn woorden „frustratie”. Grapperhaus was zelf ook niet vies van beledigende opmerkingen , bleek woensdag tijdens zijn verhoor. Hij zei onder meer over de Eerste Kamer „diepe minachting” te hebben „voor deze geriatrische beunhazerij”. Me tulemme pyytämään ne rahat takaisin, vaikkakin hieman myöhässä! hän lisäsi. Trump syytti edeltäjänsä presidentti Joe Bidenin hallintoa. articles.title: Pentagon Orders Mass Cyber Vulnerability Scans
articles.content: SPONSORED FEATURE: Boards want to know if they're less exposed than last quarter. Patching metrics aren't the solution Robin Birtstone Robin Birtstone Published thu 3 Sep 2026 // 16:00 UTC A decade or two ago, board executives asked "why should I care about cybersecurity?" Five years ago, they were asking "Are you patching our software vulnerabilities?" Now, they're starting to ask: "Are we actually secure?" They might want a simple 'yes' or 'no' initially, but eventually they'll say the most dreaded thing of all, and it'll be a demand, not a question: "Prove it". Traditional vulnerability management and patching, won't survive that conversation. It's why a relatively new approach is gaining traction: Continuous Threat Exposure Management (CTEM). What's wrong with vulnerability management We define security flaws using Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs), and we tell each other how bad they are by assigning the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) to them. There are three problems with that. There's a firehose of CVEs, the CVSS scores aren't helpful when triaging them, and AI is about to make the whole thing much worse. CISOs are drowning in CVEs. The industry has spent decades creating tools that churn out vulnerability data and others that consume it. Few if any tell you which vulnerabilities an attacker could use to hurt you in your environment. The volume of CVEs is making traditional vulnerability management (patch it and forget it) less tractable every year, says Drew Vanover, principal security strategist at Horizon3. "Think about the last patch release that Microsoft put out," he says. "There were over 500 fixes in one patch cycle. That is incomprehensible. Nobody is going to be able to go through, vet, prioritize, and deploy all of those in a way that is truly considered safe." The number of CVEs created each year has been soaring , putting more pressure on the US’ National Institute for Standards and Technology's National Vulnerability Database, which has now been backlogged for years. NIST threw up its hands in April and effectively declared CVE bankruptcy . The US Department of Commerce highlighted the second issue (that current severity metrics aren't useful) as part of a  report this May. Aside from launching a zinger at the NIST by saying that the NVD was poorly managed, it also suggested that it stop assigning CVSS scores altogether. These are highly subjective, it said. They also depend on exactly what the exposed system is doing in a particular organization's infrastructure. Is a critical severity score in a product important if only one sandboxed system ever interacts with it? Or could an attacker chain three apparently innocuous vulns to cause damage that a business executive would care about? AI will make vulnerability management harder These complex problems are a headache, but AI is about to turn it into a full-on migraine. Frontier LLMs like Claude's Mythos are already surfacing zero-days at scale, heralding a flood of CVEs. They don't just find bugs at scale; they also work much more quickly than their human counterparts to create and weaponize exploits. This makes it even more important that organizations patch the right bugs quickly. The Cloud Security Alliance now describes an asymmetric vulnerability cycle in which attackers can use AI to discover and exploit vulnerabilities more quickly, (increasingly before patches are even released), while organizations are taking longer to patch them. What is CTEM? Something has to change. Gartner figured this out in 2023, when it named CTEM a top cybersecurity trend. This is a way of staying on top of your vulnerabilities by triaging them properly. To do that, you have to go beyond the technical implications of a security flaw and understand what it really means for your business. Gartner lays out five steps to CTEM: ●  Scoping  Find the assets that carry significant business impact and prioritize them. ●  Discovery Find how they're exposed by analyzing their weaknesses in depth. ●  Prioritization  Rank those exposures based on real business risk. ●  Validation  Test out the vulnerabilities to see if they're exploitable. ●  Mobilization Fix them with a proper incident response plan. How automated pen testing helps manage vulnerabilities This approach promises to nail the security flaws that matter to an organization, but it's also more complex than traditional vulnerability management. It needs automation, which is what Horizon3 is providing with NodeZero. Scoping out systems is a commodity practice these days. So is discovery. Horizon3 is leaving those to partners so it can focus on the parts of the CTEM framework that aren't yet easy for customers to solve. Those are prioritization by business impact, and mobilization. NodeZero runs penetration tests across an organization's infrastructure and documents the exploitable paths with evidence a defender can follow. The output is the wheat sifted from the chaff; a shorter list of exposures that security teams and developers can focus on. The impressive part here is the chain-of-attack behavior. NodeZero probes for weaknesses, exploits them, and then pivots based on what it finds. This means it adapts to the environment to extend its attack, just as a real attacker adapts attacks and moves laterally through systems. This approach is based on a deterministic machine learning expert system rather than a general LLM, explains Vanover. "A good analogy is to think about the medical profession," he says. "A GP is your general LLM trying to cover everything. They know a little bit about a lot, but they aren't the experts, and that's where you start having hallucinations and guesses and misses." The company only uses generative AI for specific tasks. Using it to parse a two petabyte S3 blob looking for sensitive data or identifying high-value credentials, with data staying inside the customer's boundary via AWS Bedrock, for example. What it doesn't do is run amok spawning rogue agents in your system. Vanover says the value here is in proving that you've clobbered load-bearing security bugs. "If we say that we can exploit something, it's because we did, and we'll show you the proof in the platform," he says. The next step is closing the loop by retesting the exploit after it's been dealt with. Teams get to close tickets because NodeZero can no longer traverse the attack path. That is a testable definition of "fixed" and one that translates into a risk metric a CFO can read. Horizon3 also wants to solve customers' tool sprawl problems with a single product that handles all of the heavy CTEM lifting. A common failure mode of enterprise CTEM programs is a stack of vendors whose handoffs create precisely the blind spots the framework was meant to eliminate. That disappears when it's all under one service. Is automated penetration testing safe? CISOs might be nervous letting an autonomous penetration testing system loose on production systems. It sounds like something that could break running processes. Why not just test against a digital twin instead? Testing in production is the safest way to find bugs, retorts Vanover. That's because environments drift frequently, especially in an agile world driven by short development sprints and automated changes to code. If a user changes a password or a team pushes a feature fragment, a digital twin system won't reflect reality. So Horizon3 focuses on strong production guardrails instead. "I don't need to ransom your system to prove to you that I can ransom it," Vanover says. "If I can get on the system, install a remote access tool, create a file, encrypt the file, and delete that file, I've just proven that I can ransom your system." He says Horizon3 has run more than 320,000 production tests across customer organizations. These include some that are especially nervous about what's poking around in their systems, such as the NSA and the largest medical records processor on the planet, along with a couple of large healthcare providers. Where can I start with CTEM? Gartner's CTEM framework is powerful, but it might also be daunting for CISOs. Vanover advises them to begin by picking one thing and doing it well. "No organization is going to implement CTEM in a year. That is a recipe for failure," he says. "Break it down. Look at places for the low-hanging fruit." You could do worse than look at what systems are actually reachable instead of blindly trusting an asset inventory that might be out of date. The race is on to embrace CTEM, because metrics like the number of patches applied won't satisfy the board for much longer. They don't describe how much exploitable surface still exists. The point of running the CTEM loop is to move reporting from activity to outcomes, so that the board gets to see fewer exploitable paths and a smaller blast radius. The new goal is to prove that a security control worked, not just that you paid for it. Want to operationalize CTEM but don’t know where to start?
